blocks.text: P-tuning is a PEFT method that learns continuous, trainable vectors to prepend to the model input, rather than relying on hand written discrete word prompts, using a small neural network called a prompt encoder to produce those vectors during training.

It sits closely alongside prompt tuning and prefix tuning, both covered elsewhere in this module, and understanding what specifically distinguishes p-tuning from those related methods helps clarify when each one is the more natural choice.
1. What P-Tuning Adds to Prompt Tuning

blocks.alt: Discrete word prompts are compared against continuous learned vectors

blocks.text: Where a hand written prompt uses actual words, discrete tokens chosen from the model vocabulary, p-tuning instead learns continuous vectors that do not correspond to any real word at all, free to take on whatever numeric values training finds most useful, unconstrained by the vocabulary.
2. Continuous Prompts, Not Discrete Words

This continuous representation gives p-tuning more flexibility than a prompt limited to real vocabulary words, since the learned vectors can settle anywhere in the embedding space during training, rather than being restricted to positions that correspond to an actual word.
3. The Prompt Encoder

blocks.alt: Random initialization passes through a prompt encoder to produce refined prompt vectors

blocks.text: Rather than training the prompt vectors completely independently of each other, p-tuning passes them through a small neural network, the prompt encoder, often a simple architecture like a small recurrent network, which helps the individual prompt vectors influence each other and produces more stable, better performing prompts than training each vector in complete isolation.

code.content:
# A simplified p-tuning setup, conceptually
prompt_vectors = prompt_encoder(random_initial_vectors)
full_input = concatenate(prompt_vectors, real_input_embeddings)
output = frozen_base_model(full_input)

blocks.text: 4. Where the Learned Vectors Get Inserted

blocks.alt: Learned prompt vectors combine with the real input embedding before the model forward pass

blocks.text: The learned continuous vectors are placed at the start of the input sequence, ahead of the actual real input, so the frozen model processes them as if they were extra context, even though they were never real text at all.
5. P-Tuning vs Prefix Tuning

blocks.alt: Prefix tuning inserts learned vectors at every layer while p-tuning focuses mainly on the input layer

blocks.text: Prefix tuning, covered as its own topic in this module, inserts learned vectors at every layer of the network, while the original p-tuning approach focuses primarily on the input embedding layer, a narrower but simpler intervention point.

blocks.text: 6. P-Tuning v2, Applying Prompts at Every Layer

blocks.alt: P-tuning v1 extends into p-tuning v2, which applies learned vectors at every layer too

blocks.text: A later version, p-tuning v2, closes the gap with prefix tuning by inserting learned continuous vectors at every layer of the network rather than just the input, improving performance on a wider range of tasks and model sizes than the original input only approach.
7. Training Only the Prompt Encoder Parameters

blocks.alt: Only the prompt encoder parameters actually train

blocks.text: As with every PEFT method covered in this module, the base model stays entirely frozen, only the prompt encoder and the learned vectors it produces get updated during training, keeping the trainable parameter count small relative to the full model.
8. Strengths of P-Tuning

P-tuning tends to perform noticeably better than simple prompt tuning, particularly on smaller models, since the prompt encoder helps the learned vectors coordinate with each other in a way that independently trained prompt embeddings cannot.
9. Choosing P-Tuning Among PEFT Options

blocks.alt: Working with smaller models is a case where p-tuning tends to help more

blocks.text: P-tuning is a reasonable choice when working with smaller models where prompt tuning alone underperforms, or when a lightweight, input focused intervention is preferred over methods like LoRA that modify weights throughout the network, though LoRA, covered in the dedicated next module, remains the more commonly reached for default for many fine-tuning projects today.
Worked Example

A team fine-tuning a smaller model finds plain prompt tuning produces inconsistent results, the learned prompt embeddings do not seem to coordinate well with each other. Switching to p-tuning, adding a small prompt encoder network to produce the learned vectors instead of training them independently, produces noticeably more stable and higher quality results on the same task and model size.
Common Mistakes

items: Confusing p-tuning with plain prompt tuning, missing the role the prompt encoder plays
Expecting p-tuning to perform as well as prefix tuning on larger models without moving to p-tuning v2
Forgetting the base model needs to stay frozen while only the prompt encoder trains
Choosing p-tuning for a task that would benefit more from a weight modifying method like LoRA

blocks.text: Practice

Compare, in your own words, what changes between plain prompt tuning and p-tuning, specifically what role the added prompt encoder plays that independently trained prompt embeddings would not provide on their own.
Key Takeaway

P-tuning learns continuous prompt vectors through a small prompt encoder network rather than training them independently, producing more stable results than plain prompt tuning, particularly for smaller models, with p-tuning v2 extending this idea to every layer of the network to close the gap with prefix tuning.
